CLIPPER SHIP "SOVEREIGN OF THE SEAS
The front cover of this menu is a reproduction of an authentic Currier & Ives clipper ship print.
Currier & Ives, known as the "Printmakers of America", graphically preserved the glorious clipper
ship era in a magnificent series of clipper ship prints. This print, one of a series, is being reproduced
through the courtesy of The Museum of the City of New York.
The clipper ship "Sovereign of the Seas," launched in 1852, influenced the design of all future
clippers. She was built with almost a flat bottomed hull to allow for greater cargo carrying capacity,
while maintaining speed. Many of the world's ship builders claimed that this was impossible to
achieve. On her maiden run to San Francisco, with a mainmast that reached over 200 feet into the
sky, and able to carry more than 12,000 yards of canvas, she made San Francisco in 103 days. To
report such record speeds was considered fantastic and incredible. It convinced the most skeptical
of the value of flat bottoms for speed. On her maiden voyage, one of the passengers wrote in his
diary, "It was fearful to see the topmasts bend as she beat around the Horn. We hardly dared look
aloft lest we should see the canvas blown away." To cap it off she then broke the record from
New York to Liverpool, making the run in 13 days, 13½ hours. "Sovereign of the Seas" reported
the highest rate of speed ever achieved by a sailing ship-22 knots. The fastest of today's ocean
liners steam along at about 31.5 knots.
Like Pan Am's modern Clippers* of the air, the early clipper ships traveled the lanes of com-
merce to all the far places of the world ... to Japan... to Australia ... and, in the days of the great
gold rush, from America's east coast, around Cape Horn, South America, to California. Our current
equipment... the Clipper feet of the Twentieth Century ... consists of the finest commercial
aircraft ever developed—aircraft that have helped us establish an unparalleled record for safety,
speed and service.
